items.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, June 4, 2020 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: when I shook Woody Herman’s hand and met Mel Lewis

ctx.x: Before we close I wanted to just say again, you know you were at Hamilton, I’m not good with how long ago, maybe two years ago, and that was such a terrific concert musically but also the fact that when the concert was done all these junior high kids, like, “Oh, could we go on the stage?” And indeed, I mean I just got such a kick out of that, interacting with you and you were so kind to them. And I know they won’t forget that.

Yeah. Well I hope so. I mean you don’t think about it when you’re in the moment but when I think back to you know when I was eleven and got to go on Buddy Rich’s bus to say hi, like to me it’s like it was yesterday or when I shook Woody Herman’s hand and met Mel Lewis, and saw Count Basie in his wheelchair outside Carnegie Hall last time I saw them play. Just, “Hi Mr. Basie.” And he’s like, “Hi,” you know. Any of those interactions to me with people that I love so. Obviously I’m not elevating myself to any
standards like the people I just mentioned but just that somebody enjoyed the concert and wanted to talk to us. It makes a difference.

items.title: Sherrie Maricle interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001 [interview 1 of 2]
items.q: Well, Mel Lewis is one of my absolute idols. I think he swings.

ctx.x: Do you have a list of must-listen-to drummers for young players?

Well, Mel Lewis is one of my absolute idols. I think he swings. Big band drummers I divide into two categories, Mel Lewis for sure and I love Buddy Rich, I always loved Buddy Rich. He’s like one of the, you know you can pick out the geniuses like Oscar Peterson on the piano and Buddy, like people who do, and Art Tatum, people who could play what nobody will ever be able to duplicate what these people have done, and he’s one of those. I love Jeff Hamilton right now who is a drummer in Los Angeles, one of my…
What’s the IAJE — do they have a mission to increase the audience for jazz as well as the players?
